sentences.text: Knoetschkesuchus was a small atoposaurid crocodylomorph that lived during the Late Jurassic in Germany and Portugal.
Both species of this animal walked on four legs using long and slender limbs.
The skull was relatively short, with the snout comprising 47% of skull length in K. langenbergensis and 42% in K. guimarotae.
An oval-shaped opening in the skull known as the antorbital fenestra was small, measuring only 9% of the eye socket's length.
The pterygoid bone at the bottom of the skull is approximately twice as wide as it is long.
The side of the dentary bone is pitted, with the pits being much denser in K. langenbergensis than in K. guimarotae.
Both species possess only two distinct types of teeth, a trait unique among atoposaurids.
K. guimarotae was very small, reaching a maximum length of only 55 centimeters.
Some specimens show marks of scavenging, indicating evidence of having been scavenged by other animals.
Two species of Knoetschkesuchus are known: K. langenbergensis described by Schwartz et al. in 2017, and K. guimarotae originally classified as Theriosuchus guimarotae.
The genus Knoetschkesuchus was established by Schwarz et al. in 2017.
The type species of the genus Knoetschkesuchus is K. langenbergensis.
The two species of Knoetschkesuchus are K. langenbergensis and K. guimarotae, the latter originally named Theriosuchus guimarotae.
The species Knoetschkesuchus guimarotae was named based on over 400 specimens, including several partial skeletons.
Fossils of Knoetschkesuchus langenbergensis were found in the Langenberg Quarry in the Harz Mountains near Goslar, Lower Saxony, Germany.
Knoetschkesuchus guimarotae originates from the lignite layers of the Guimarota quarry near Leiria, Portugal.
Specimens of K. langenbergensis were first preliminarily described in a 2006 paper by Hans-Volker Karl et al. and initially referred to the genus Theriosuchus.

The fossils of K. langenbergensis include a partial adult skeleton with a skull, a complete juvenile skull, an isolated angular bone, an isolated left dentary, an isolated femur, an isolated metatarsal, and a partial skeleton with osteoderms, vertebrae, and ribs.
Researchers Schwarz and colleagues assigned the species K. guimarotae to the genus Knoetschkesuchus, noting it was originally classified as a species of Theriosuchus.
Knoetschkesuchus primarily fed on small prey such as invertebrates, amphibians, and mammals.
Knoetschkesuchus was a small predator that primarily ate invertebrates and possibly small vertebrates like amphibians and mammals.
Both species of Knoetschkesuchus were formerly classified as belonging to the genus Theriosuchus.
Phylogenetic analysis consistently found that Atoposauridae, represented by Knoetschkesuchus, Theriosuchus, and Alligatorium, forms a monophyletic clade.
The parent group of Knoetschkesuchus is the family Atoposauridae.
Knoetschkesuchus is classified within the class Reptilia.
The deposits containing Knoetschkesuchus langenbergensis fossils date to the Upper Kimmeridgian stage of the Jurassic.
The Guimarota strata containing K. guimarotae fossils have been dated to the Kimmeridgian based on fossil ostracods.
During the Kimmeridgian, Europe consisted of scattered archipelagos surrounded by the shallow inland Tethys Ocean.
The Langenberg Quarry where K. langenbergensis was found is located in the Lower Saxony Basin, associated with the Rhenisch, Bohemian, and London-Brabant Massifs.
The Guimarota locality where K. guimarotae was found is in the eastern Lusitanian Basin, part of the Iberian Meseta.
K. langenbergensis differs from the proposed Theriosuchus diagnosis in four out of nine traits, a difference cited by Schwarz et al. as the basis for separating Knoetschkesuchus into its own genus.
Some researchers have attributed specimens assigned to K. langenbergensis to another species of Theriosuchus, T. pusillus.
